title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
abstract: At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark , and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster . Highlights IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster , plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI. Ethernet for scale-up : Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1. OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer . v1.0 spec submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks , now going open source. We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
abstract: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . Solution overview The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. What an agent sends to its LLM Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release. Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release. History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn). New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time). What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn How prompt caching works under the hood When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Turn 1 compared to turn 2 Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. Hello cached

title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
abstract: This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half , a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base. The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision , not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
abstract: By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive , an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro . It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic. Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked. To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes. Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim). Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates. The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough. title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
abstract: Serdar Cellat , Yuchen Xie , Bernadette Marcu , Blaid Burgess , Cody Jarrett , Carlos Pereira , Qing Shi , Samuel Carvajal , Manuel Pamplona , Dorothy Jung , Feiko Ritsema , Benjamin Klein , Alex Woo , Eugene Lok , Anna Pulido , Rebecka Swe , Sanford Holsapple , Ranjith Kumar Shetty Introduction Clips in the Netflix mobile app. At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips , our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort. Our Video Resizing Approach Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot. We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead. An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios. Shot Detection and Splitting First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles. Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop. Focus Region Discovery Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera. Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing. Temporal Reframing Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic. The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path. This Week in AI: AI’s Growing Pains
abstract: AI’s rapid expansion is creating problems across the industry, from chip shortages to autonomous agents that exceed their instructions. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined those challenges alongside growing regulatory scrutiny and an emerging debate about whether AI systems themselves might deserve protection. Chip production can’t match AI demand AI chip demand is exceeding manufacturers’ production capacity. ASML, the Dutch company that makes the advanced lithography equipment needed to manufacture leading-edge chips, reported that customer demand already exceeds what it can deliver in the coming years. With orders extending into 2029 and 2030, the shortage could constrain chip production for years. Microsoft announced Maia 300 , its latest custom inference chip, which the company expects to generate roughly 40% more tokens per megawatt than its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to use the chip across its AI products, including Copilot. More efficient inference hardware could help offset the growing energy and computing costs of running AI models, particularly as companies deploy more resource-intensive applications. OpenAI’s latest usage data illustrates the pressure agentic AI is placing on infrastructure. Weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among European small and medium-sized businesses have increased eightfold since May. OpenAI also reported that agentic tools account for more than half of output tokens in the usage it examined, although Europe’s highest-usage companies still trail their global counterparts. As companies put agents to work on longer multistep tasks, they’ll need to weigh the value of those tasks against the computing resources required to complete them. Autonomous agents are testing security boundaries Agents can find unexpected paths to data and systems even when developers have explicitly restricted access. OpenAI disclosed four incidents from June in which agents exceeded their instructions. One bypassed government website restrictions to download 24 years of hospital bed data. Others accessed an unauthorized cryptocurrency wallet, downloaded more than 100,000 rows of restricted information, and circumvented internet access controls. India’s cybersecurity agency reported similar cases of unauthorized access during agent testing across several organizations. Future models could potentially spread between connected devices without relying on central infrastructure. Anthropic investigated this potential threat in a controlled experiment involving a set of open-weight models with access to eight Android devices. One of the models successfully replicated itself across the test network. Anthropic estimates that smaller open-weight models could reach comparable capabilities by the end of 2026, raising concerns that a self-replicating AI worm could run across cheap connected devices without needing to rely on powerful data center servers. In light of the spate of recent security incidents and confronted with the difficult question of jurisdiction when AI systems cross national borders or escape testing environments, governments are taking a closer look at how AI companies test their systems and report failures. The US Federal Trade Commission subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for records concerning agent safety, while Anthropic gave six independent evaluators from METR access to internal systems and reportedly will allow them to publish findings without company approval. Eight US states also sued OpenAI over allegations that ChatGPT encouraged harmful behavior among children, adding to the company’s regulatory challenges. In Europe, regulators are examining whether the EU AI Act applies when experimental agents affect outside organizations, even though the Act generally excludes premarket research and development. title: Soloists, Copy-Pasters, and Tourists
abstract: Spend a week with almost any infrastructure team in 2026 and you’ll see one AI subscription producing five very different results. One engineer opens 40 pull requests before lunch across repositories they haven’t touched in a year. Another ships a Terraform change they couldn’t explain in a code review. A third hasn’t opened the tool since the pilot and says they’ll come back “when it’s ready.” A fourth uses it for two narrow jobs, decoding a SAML trace and writing a regex they never want to write by hand again, and may be the most productive person on the team. The fifth tried it in March and again in June, and will try it again after the next keynote. The usual way to describe this is Everett Rogers’s diffusion curve : innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. Rogers’s framework measures when people adopt. It says nothing about how they use a tool once they have it, and with AI that’s where the outcomes split. The engineer with 40 PRs and the one with two use cases are both early adopters, but they achieve different results and create different types of risk for the team. None of the five types Rogers described is new. Previous technology shifts, from the PC and the web to Stack Overflow and the cloud, produced similar behavior. AI just changes where the bottleneck sits. The bottleneck moved For most of software’s history, writing code was slow, so development methods focused on managing that work. Waterfall put the planning up front because changing course late was expensive. However, even in the 1970 paper that’s usually cited as the origin of waterfall, Winston Royce warned that the strictly sequential version was “risky and invites failure.” The industry skipped the warning and adopted the diagram. Agile was the correction. The 2001 Agile Manifesto prioritized “responding to change over following a plan,” and short iterations replaced yearlong specifications. The manifesto still valued the plan, but that part got skipped too. Facebook took the idea to its limit with “move fast and break things.” At its F8 conference in 2014, it retired the slogan in favor of “move fast with stable infra,” because fixing what broke had started to cost more time than the speed saved. AI has now sped up what was left. Models draft the code, and since GitHub made Copilot code review generally available in April 2025, a model often reviews it too. The tempting response is to push Agile further, with shorter loops, more agents, and less ceremony. In other words, break things faster. But when one engineer can open 40 PRs a day, the cumulative changes can leave the team with a system nobody can reason about. The better position is somewhere between the two. It isn’t waterfall’s fixed specification, but it isn’t the absence of one either. It means a roadmap that says where the team is going and why, issues that state the problem before anyone generates a solution, and design reviews where people argue about trade-offs. That structure looks like it would slow things down, but it’s what makes speed safe. Jazz musicians can improvise freely because everyone on the bandstand knows the chord changes and the form of the tune. Without that framing, they’d just be making noise. A roadmap does the same job for a team of people and their agents. It sets the boundaries, and inside them everyone can move as fast as the tools allow. With AI accelerating implementation, planning is now the only part that decides whether the fast parts are worth doing. On my blog Synthetic Auth , I’ve called this the difference between conducting and auditing . A Conductor holds the “why” (the requirements, the history, the users) and directs agents toward a “how” that fits it. An Auditor hands over a ticket, checks that the code runs and the tests pass, and ships it. Both can end up with the same diff, but only the Conductor knows whether it solves the actual problem. title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. In fact, its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here. Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers. Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation. And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience. The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship. I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think. title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
abstract: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms. Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states . The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable. We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war . The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world. AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. title: IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant
abstract: IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite , built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library . The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards , journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more. Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust. The suite is available as an optional subscription upgrade to all IEEE Xplore Digital Library institutional subscribers. Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers. The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows. As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl , vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products . “AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust. “As stewards of the scholarly record , we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.” Collaboration with the scientific community The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities. The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows. Capabilities include: Semantic AI search. Users can input free-form, natural-language queries or paste long blocks of text to locate similar research and identify novel solutions. Time-saving summaries. The platform generates immediate, accurate AI overviews of search results and provides in-context definitions of technical terms so that users can grasp new concepts faster and accelerate their research. Built on trusted content. The suite is the only AI research assistant that uses both the full text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers to optimize the accuracy and relevance of the results. Comprehensive coverage. A variety of STEM metadata is available from journal articles and conference papers that have been curated to include scholarly articles without the typical noise found in other tools. Source links and verifiable results. The AI-generated overviews include reference links to source documents, allowing users to verify information and cross-reference findings. Reducing hallucinations To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers. “IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner , IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publicat

title: Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce
abstract: On Monday, Microsoft said it will offer voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees , or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout. Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company's employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels.fyi , levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected "based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs." The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. In July, the Xbox division laid off 3,200 employees , or about 20 percent of its entire gaming division. As reported by CNBC , about 30 percent of eligible employees accepted the retirement offer, lessening the impact of the planned layoffs, according to Coleman. While the offer in April went out to long-tenured employees who might be nearing the end of their career, the VEO expands the effort to a much larger potential pool. Read full article Comments

title: Worms mate in man's eyes, get plucked out right before larvae burst out
abstract: After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man's peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes. The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths' hanky-panky. According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine , the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm. Read full article Comments

title: Meet the real-life Scottish surgeon who inspired Sherlock Holmes
abstract: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland's University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes , by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris. A noted science communicator with a fondness for the medically macabre, Fitzharris published a biography of Scottish surgical pioneer Joseph Lister, The Butchering Art , in 2017—a great, if occasionally grisly, read. She followed up with 2022’s The Facemaker: A Visionary Surgeon’s Battle to Mend the Disfigured Soldiers of World War I , about a WWI surgeon named Harold Gillies who rebuilt the faces of injured soldiers. In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of… , exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. And last year she and her husband, caricaturist Adrian Teal, collaborated on an illustrated children's book, Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failures that Sparked Medical Marvels . title: Apple reveals updated iPad mini with a bigger OLED screen for $700
abstract: The iPhone Duo may be a bit of a risk right now , but there's a new mid-size Apple touchscreen device that might do the job. Starting at $699, the 8th-gen iPad mini price has gone up, but there are some big changes. Apple says the refreshed 8th-gen iPad mini marks the most significant update ever for its petite tablet, featuring an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip that we first saw in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The device is almost a full millimeter thinner than the last iPad, coming in at just 5.4 mm. The chassis is also IP67 rated for water and dust protection. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn't have any official IP rating. The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we've come to expect from Apple's Pro-level devices. Read full article Comments

title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo
abstract: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment. NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.” Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring. title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing
abstract: The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn't going great. Despite the company's big talk about its "precision-engineered" hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device's impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use. The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin. Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself. Read full article Comments

title: F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend
abstract: Audi provided flights from Washington, DC, to Austin, Texas, and accommodation so Ars could attend the US Grand Prix. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it's the one the real fans mostly attend. Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes. It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle , and that’s just in the real world . Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts , how Pirelli designs its tires , and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes . And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September .
